L8@P0: Abstract
L9@P0: Particle filters are not compatible with automatic differentiation due to the presence
L10@P0: of discrete resampling steps. While known
L11@P0: estimators for the score function, based on
L12@P0: Fisher’s identity, can be computed using particle filters, up to this point they required
L13@P0: manual implementation. In this paper we
L14@P0: show that such estimators can be computed
L15@P0: using automatic differentiation, after introducing a simple correction to the particle weights.
L16@P0: This correction utilizes the stop-gradient operator and does not modify the particle filter
L17@P0: operation on the forward pass, while also being cheap and easy to compute. Surprisingly,
L18@P0: with the same correction automatic differentiation also produces good estimators for gradients of expectations under the posterior. We
L19@P0: can therefore regard our method as a general
L20@P0: recipe for making particle filters differentiable.
L21@P0: We additionally show that it produces desired
L22@P0: estimators for second-order derivatives and
L23@P0: how to extend it to further reduce variance
L24@P0: at the expense of additional computation.
L25@P0: 1 Introduction
L26@P0: Sequential latent variable models can be learned by gradient ascent, applying automatic differentiation (AD)
L27@P0: to the log-marginal likelihood estimators obtained with
L28@P0: particle filters. Examples include robotic localization
L29@P0: [Jonschkowski et al., 2018], world-modeling in reinforcement learning [Igl et al., 2018], and deep generative modeling of music and speech [Maddison et al.,
L30@P0: 2017]. Unfortunately, the discrete resampling steps
L31@P0: Preliminary work.
L32@P0: allowing particle filters to adaptively focus computational resources on promising paths cause problems for
L33@P0: automatic differentiation, with the usual algorithms
L34@P0: producing gradient estimators that suffer from excessive variance. In current practice, the dependence of
L35@P0: the resampling probabilities on model parameters is
L36@P0: typically ignored [Le et al., 2018a, Maddison et al.,
L37@P0: 2017, Naesseth et al., 2018], introducing bias that was
L38@P0: shown not to vanish asymptotically [Corenflos et al.,
L39@P0: 2021] and impede learning.
L40@P0: Several recent articles [Corenflos et al., 2021, Zhu et al.,
L41@P0: 2020, Karkus et al., 2018] have proposed continuous
L42@P0: relaxations of the discrete resampling steps to avoid this
L43@P0: problem, with different trade-offs and varying degrees
L44@P0: of complexity, as discussed in detail in Section 6. At
L45@P0: the same time, there exist consistent estimators of the
L46@P0: gradient of log-marginal likelihood that can be obtained
L47@P0: with usual discrete resampling [Poyiadjis et al., 2011],
L48@P0: but until now these could not be obtained by applying
L49@P0: AD to the log-marginal likelihood estimator produced
L50@P0: by a particle filter.
L51@P0: In this work we show that a simple and computationally inexpensive modification to an otherwise entirely
L52@P0: standard “basic” particle filter implementation allows
L53@P0: AD to produce the estimators derived by Poyiadjis
L54@P0: et al. [2011]. The modification, shown in Algorithm 1,
L55@P0: can be thought of as stopping the gradients of weights
L56@P0: flowing into the resampling distribution, instead directing them into the resulting weights. Crucially, it does
L57@P0: not modify the estimators produced by the particle
L58@P0: filter on the forward pass, only changing the gradients
L59@P0: computed by AD. We also show that with our modification AD produces sensible, easy to interpret, and
L60@P0: consistent estimators for gradients of expectations under the posterior, which are additionally unbiased if the
L61@P0: estimator obtained on the forward pass is unbiased. We
L62@P0: can therefore regard our modification as a general technique for making a particle filter differentiable, without
L63@P0: modifying its behavior on the forward pass. While existing differentiable resampling mechanisms have their
L64@P0: merits, the simplicity of our approach is unmatched,

L67@P1: sophisticated alternatives.
L68@P1: Additionally, in Section 4 we show that our results extend to higher-order derivatives computed by repeated
L69@P1: AD and that the same method applies to marginal
L70@P1: particle filters [Klaas et al., 2012], recovering the more
L71@P1: expensive but lower variance estimator proposed by
L72@P1: Poyiadjis et al. [2011]. We also briefly discuss the problem of jointly learning a proposal distribution with the

L10@P0: Abstract—An analytic solution to the multi-target Bayes recursion known as the δ-Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (δGLMB) filter has been recently proposed in [1]. As a sequel
L11@P0: to [1], this paper details efficient implementations of theδ-
L12@P0: GLMB multi-target tracking filter. Each iteration of this filter
L13@P0: involves an update operation and a prediction operation, both of
L14@P0: which result in weighted sums of multi-target exponentials with
L15@P0: intractably large number of terms. To truncate these sums, the
L16@P0: ranked assignment and K-th shortest path algorithms are used
L17@P0: in the update and prediction, respectively, to determine the most
L18@P0: significant terms without exhaustively computing all of the terms.
L19@P0: In addition, using tools derived from the same framework, such
L20@P0: as probability hypothesis density filtering, we present inexpensive
L21@P0: (relative to theδ-GLMB filter) look-ahead strategies to reduce
L22@P0: the number of computations. Characterization of theL
L23@P0: 1-error in
L24@P0: the multi-target density arising from the truncation is presented.
L25@P0: Index Terms—Random finite set, marked point process, conjugate prior, Bayesian estimation, target tracking.
L26@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L27@P0: Multi-target filtering involves the on-line estimation of an
L28@P0: unknown and time-varying number of targets and their individual states from a sequence of observations [2]–[4]. While the
L29@P0: term multi-target filtering is often used interchangeably with
L30@P0: multi-target tracking, there is a subtle difference. In multitarget tracking we are also interested in the trajectories of
L31@P0: the targets (indeed, real multi-target tracking systems require
L32@P0: track labels). This work is concerned with a Bayesian multitarget filtering solution that also provides estimates of target
L33@P0: trajectories, hence the name multi-target tracking filter.
L34@P0: The key challenges in multi-target filtering/tracking include
L35@P0: detection uncertainty, clutter, and data association uncertainty. To date, three major approaches to multi-target tracking/filtering have emerged as the main solution paradigms.
L36@P0: These are, Multiple Hypotheses Tracking (MHT), [2], [5]–
L37@P0: [7], Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) [2], [4], and
L38@P0: Random Finite Set (RFS) [3].
L39@P0: The random finite set (RFS) approach provides an elegant Bayesian formulation of the multi-target filtering/tracking
L40@P0: problem in which the collection of target states, referred to as
L41@P0: Acknowledgement: This work is supported by the Australian Research
L42@P0: Council under the Future Fellowship FT0991854 and Discovery Early Career
L43@P0: Researcher Award DE120102388
L44@P0: B.-N. Vo and B.-T. Vo are with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Curtin University, Bentley, WA 6102, Australia (email: {ba-ngu,ba-tuong}.vo@curtin.edu.au). D. Phung is with the Faculty of Science, Engineering & Built Environment, Deakin University, Geelong, VIC
L45@P0: 3220, Australia (email: dinh.phung@deakin.edu.au)
L46@P0: the multi-target state, is treated as a finite set [3], [8]. The rationale behind this representation traces back to a fundamental
L47@P0: consideration in estimation theory–estimation error [9]. This
L48@P0: mathematical framework subsequently became a very popular
L49@P0: multi-target estimation method with applications in sonar [10],
L50@P0: computer vision [11], [12], [13], [14], field robotics [15], [16],
L51@P0: [17], [18], [19] traffic monitoring [20], [21], [22], cell biology
L52@P0: [23], [13], [24], sensor network and distributed estimation [25],
L53@P0: [26], [27], [28] etc.
L54@P0: The centerpiece of the RFS approach is the Bayes multitarget filter [3], which recursively propagates the filtering
L55@P0: density of the multi-target state forward in time. This filter
L56@P0: is also a (multi-target) tracker when target identities or labels
L57@P0: are incorporated into individual target states. Due to the numerical complexity of Bayes multi-target filter, the Probability
L58@P0: Hypothesis Density (PHD) [8], Cardinalized PHD (CPHD)
L59@P0: [29], and multi-Bernoulli filters [30], [9] have been developed
L60@P0: as approximations. These filters, in principle, are not multitarget trackers because they rest on the premise that targets
L61@P0: are indistinguishable.
L62@P0: In [1], [31], the notion of labeled RFSs is introduced to
L63@P0: address target trajectories and their uniqueness. The key results
L64@P0: include conjugate priors that are closed under the ChapmanKolmogorov equation, and an analytic solution to the Bayes
L65@P0: multi-target tracking filter known as theδ-generalized labeled
L66@P0: multi-Bernoulli (δ-GLMB) filter. Although a simulation result
L67@P0: was presented to verify the solution, specific implementation
L68@P0: details were not given.
L69@P0: As a sequel to [1], the aim of this paper is to complement
L70@P0: its theoretical contributions with practical algorithms that will
L71@P0: facilitate the development of applications in signal processing
L72@P0: and related fields. In particular, we present an efficient and
L73@P0: highly parallelizable implementation of theδ-GLMB filter.
L74@P0: Each iteration of theδ-GLMB filter involves multi-target filtering and prediction densities that are weighted sums of multitarget exponentials. While these sums are expressible in closed
L75@P0: forms, the number of terms grows super-exponentially in time.
L76@P0: Furthermore, it is not tractable to exhaustively compute all the
L77@P0: terms of the multi-target densities first and then truncate by
L78@P0: discarding those deemed insignificant.
L79@P0: The key innovation is the truncation of the multi-target
L80@P0: densities without exhaustively computing all their components.
L81@P0: The multi-target filtering and prediction densities are truncated
L82@P0: using the ranked assignment andK-shortest paths algorithms,
L83@P0: respectively. Techniques such as PHD filtering are used as
L84@P0: inexpensive look-ahead strategies to drastically reduce the
L85@P0: number of calls to ranked assignment andK-shortest paths
L86@P0-1: algorithms. Moreover, we establish that truncation by discard-PREPRINT: IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON SIGNAL PROCESSING, VOL. 62, NO. 24, PP. 6554–6567, 2014 2
L87@P1: ing δ-GLMB components with small weights minimizes the
L88@P1: L1 error in the multi-target density. To our best knowledge,
L89@P1: this is the first result regarding the effect of truncation on the
L90@P1: multi-target probability law.
L91@P1: The paper is organized as follows. Background on labeled
L92@P1: RFS and the δ-GLMB filter is provided in section II. Section
L93@P1: III establishes the L1-distance between a δ-GLMB density
L94@P1: and its truncated version. Sections IV and V present efficient
L95@P1: implementations δ-GLMB filter update and prediction respectively. Section VI details the multi-target state estimation, and
L96@P1: discusses look-ahead strategies to reduce the computational
L97@P1: load. Numerical results are presented in Section VII and
L98@P1: concluding remarks are given in Section VIII.

L9@P0: ABSTRACT
L10@P0: Predicting the motion of multiple agents is necessary for planning in dynamic
L11@P0: environments. This task is challenging for autonomous driving since agents (e.g.,
L12@P0: vehicles and pedestrians) and their associated behaviors may be diverse and influence one another. Most prior work have focused on predicting independent futures
L13@P0: for each agent based on all past motion, and planning against these independent
L14@P0: predictions. However, planning against independent predictions can make it challenging to represent the future interaction possibilities between different agents,
L15@P0: leading to sub-optimal planning. In this work, we formulate a model for predicting
L16@P0: the behavior of all agents jointly, producing consistent futures that account for
L17@P0: interactions between agents. Inspired by recent language modeling approaches, we
L18@P0: use a masking strategy as the query to our model, enabling one to invoke a single
L19@P0: model to predict agent behavior in many ways, such as potentially conditioned on
L20@P0: the goal or full future trajectory of the autonomous vehicle or the behavior of other
L21@P0: agents in the environment. Our model architecture employs attention to combine
L22@P0: features across road elements, agent interactions, and time steps. We evaluate
L23@P0: our approach on autonomous driving datasets for both marginal and joint motion
L24@P0: prediction, and achieve state of the art performance across two popular datasets.
L25@P0: Through combining a scene-centric approach, agent permutation equivariant model,
L26@P0: and a sequence masking strategy, we show that our model can unify a variety of
L27@P0: motion prediction tasks from joint motion predictions to conditioned prediction.
L28@P0: 1 INTRODUCTION
L29@P0: Motion planning in a dense real-world urban environment is a mission-critical problem for deploying
L30@P0: autonomous driving technology. Autonomous driving is traditionally considered too difficult for a
L31@P0: single end-to-end learned system (Thrun et al., 2006). Thus, researchers have opted to split the task
L32@P0: into sequential sub-tasks (Zeng et al., 2019): (i) perception, (ii) motion prediction, and (iii) planning.
L33@P0: Perception is the task of detecting and tracking objects in the scene from sensors such as LiDARs
L34@P0: and cameras. Motion prediction involves predicting the futures actions of other agents in the scene.
L35@P0: Finally, planning involves creating a motion plan that navigates through dynamic environments.
L36@P0: Dividing the larger problem into sub-tasks achieves optimal performance when each sub-task is truly
L37@P0: independent. However, such a strategy breaks down when the assumption of independence does not
L38@P0: hold. For instance, the sub-tasks of motion prediction and planning are not truly independent—the
L39@P0: autonomous vehicle’s actions may significantly impact the behaviors of other agents. Similarly, the
L40@P0: behaviors of other agents may dramatically change what is a good plan. The goal of this work is
L41@P0: to take a step in the direction of unifying motion prediction and planning by developing a model
L42@P0: that can exploit varying forms of conditioning information, such as the AV’s goal, and produce joint
L43@P0: consistent predictions about the future for all agents simultaneously.
L44@P0: While the motion prediction task has traditionally been formulated around per-agent independent
L45@P0: predictions, recent datasets (Ettinger et al., 2021; Zhan et al., 2019) have introduced interaction
L46@P0: prediction tasks that enable us to study joint future prediction (Figure 1). These interaction prediction

L55@P1: tasks require models to predict the joint futures of multiple agents: models are expected to produce

L57@P1: A naive approach to producing joint futures is to consider the exponential number of combinations of
L58@P1: marginal agent predictions. Many of the combinations are not consistent, especially when agents
L59@P1: have overlapping trajectories. We present a unified model that naturally captures the interactions
L60@P1: between agents, and can be trained as a joint model to produce scene-level consistent predictions
L61@P1: across all agents (Figure 1, right). Our model uses a scene-centric representation for all agents (Lee
L62@P1: et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2019; Casas et al., 2020a; Salzmann et al., 2020) to allow scaling to large
L63@P1: numbers of agents in dense environments. We employ a simple variant of self-attention (Vaswani
L64@P1: et al., 2017) in which the attention mechanism is efficiently factorized across the agent-time axes. The
L65@P1: resulting architecture simply alternates attention between dimensions representing time and agents
L66@P1: across the scene, resulting in a computationally-efficient, uniform, and scalable architecture.
L67@P1: We find that the resulting model, termed Scene Transformer, achieves superior performance on both
L68@P1: independent (marginal) and interactive (joint) prediction benchmarks.
